title: Serenade for Strings in E minor
hook: A wedding-anniversary present for his wife, and the first of his works Elgar said he liked.

painting.title: The Long Engagement
painting.pairingNote: A poor young curate and his fiancée in a spring wood, kept apart by money and family; Alice Roberts’s family disinherited her for marrying Elgar, and this music was his anniversary present to her three years later.

facts: In 1886 Alice Roberts, the daughter of a major-general, began piano accompaniment lessons with a young Worcester violin teacher, Edward Elgar. He was eight years younger, a Catholic, and worked in his father’s music shop; her family disapproved, and she was disinherited. They married on 8 May 1889.

By 1891 Elgar could not earn enough from composing in London, and the family moved back to Malvern, where he taught and conducted local ensembles. He wrote the Serenade there in the spring of 1892, as a present for their third wedding anniversary. On the manuscript of a piano-duet version he noted that “Braut”, German for “bride”, meaning Alice, “helped a great deal to make these little tunes”.

It is the first of his works that Elgar said he was happy with: “I like ‘em (the first thing I ever did)”. A publisher turned it down as “practically unsaleable”; it was first played in public in Antwerp in 1896, and in Britain only in 1899, the year the *Enigma Variations* made him famous.
It is music for strings alone: violins, violas, cellos and double basses, often divided into more parts. Three short movements, about thirteen minutes in all.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a gentle, rocking morning song (I), a long, singing slow movement at the centre (II), a swaying finale that turns back to the first movement’s tune (III).

movements.heading: Allegro piacevole
movements.summary: *Piacevole* means “pleasantly”. The movement rocks gently in a slow two, like a lullaby or a morning song, and never raises its voice for long. A small figure in the violas starts it, keeps coming back, and ends it.

mainIdeas.name: The viola figure
mainIdeas.description: a short, tapping, dotted rhythm, heard alone at the start.

mainIdeas.name: The main tune
mainIdeas.description: a soft, rocking melody in E minor in the first violins, more wistful than sad.

mainIdeas.name: The middle tune
mainIdeas.description: a wider, arching melody that turns to the major, dips briefly into the minor and settles again.

stops.hear: The violas alone, a short tapping figure, quiet and light
stops.happening: The figure that frames the whole movement

stops.hear: The violins enter with a gentle, rocking tune over the violas’ tapping
stops.happening: The main tune, in E minor

stops.hear: The tune repeats and grows a little warmer; the lower strings fill out the harmony
stops.happening: The first section rounds itself off

stops.hear: A broader melody, in a brighter key, climbs and falls in long arches; for a moment it clouds over into the minor
stops.happening: The middle section

stops.hear: The tapping figure in the violas again, then the rocking tune
stops.happening: The opening returns

stops.hear: A new, tender phrase in the major, made from the shape of the opening
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The viola figure one more time, and a soft close
stops.happening: The movement ends quietly

notice: Count how often the viola figure comes back. It is the movement’s signature, and it is heard both at the start and at the very end.
Listen for the moment the middle melody dips into the minor. It lasts only a few bars, and then the music relaxes into the major again.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Sinfonia of London of 1962 was not a concert orchestra but a band of London’s leading players, founded in 1955 to record film music; in 1958 it recorded the soundtrack of Hitchcock’s *Vertigo*. Barbirolli’s tempos are broad: this movement takes almost four minutes, where many performances take about three and a half.

movements.heading: Larghetto
movements.summary: The heart of the work, and its longest movement. After a short introduction the first violins sing one long melody that seems to unfold without a break; the critic Ernest Newman called it one of the finest and most sustained Elgar ever wrote. The music swells to a warm climax and then closes with the phrase it began with.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction
mainIdeas.description: a short, falling phrase in the lower strings, half question, half sigh.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, slow line in the first violins, rising in waves, with the other strings moving underneath.

stops.hear: Soft, low string chords and a short phrase that falls and pauses
stops.happening: The introduction

stops.hear: The first violins begin a long, slow melody, very quietly
stops.happening: The main melody, in C major

stops.hear: The melody climbs higher; violas and cellos answer it with lines of their own
stops.happening: The melody unfolds; the inner voices move independently

stops.hear: The harmony grows restless and the sound thickens; the music presses forward
stops.happening: The middle of the movement, building

stops.hear: All the strings together at their warmest and loudest
stops.happening: The climax

stops.hear: The main melody again, calmer now
stops.happening: The melody returns

stops.hear: The falling phrase from the very beginning, now as a farewell
stops.happening: The introduction comes back to close the movement

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Long, hushed chords fading away
stops.happening: A quiet ending in C major

notice: Follow the first violins from the start of the melody to the climax. Notice how rarely the line stops for breath.
The movement ends with the phrase it began with. Listen for it in the last minute.

movements.heading: Allegretto – Come prima
movements.summary: A light, swaying finale in G major, in a lilting 12/8 time. It seems to be heading for a quick, happy ending, but near the close the rhythm slows into the 6/8 of the first movement and its rocking tune returns. The Serenade ends where it began, now in E major. *Come prima* means “as at first”.

mainIdeas.name: The finale tune
mainIdeas.description: a lilting, swaying melody, simple and good-humoured.

mainIdeas.name: The return
mainIdeas.description: the rocking main tune of the first movement, back at the end.

stops.hear: A light, swinging tune in the violins; the beat falls in long groups of three
stops.happening: The finale tune, in G major

stops.hear: The tune passes to the lower strings while the violins answer above
stops.happening: The tune is shared out

stops.hear: Warmer and fuller; a short swell, then the music relaxes
stops.happening: The middle of the movement

stops.hear: The swing slows into a gentler rocking; the first movement’s tune returns
stops.happening: *Come prima*: the opening of the work comes back

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Soft chords, settling into E major
stops.happening: The work ends quietly

notice: When the first movement’s tune returns, notice that it is in the major. The Serenade began in E minor and ends in E major.
Compare the swing of this movement with the rocking of the first. One counts in long groups of three, the other in shorter ones, and Elgar slides from one into the other.

threads.title: A present
threads.body: Elgar wrote the Serenade for Alice for their third wedding anniversary, when he was still an unknown local musician. He later said it was the first of his works he really liked.

threads.title: Strings alone
threads.body: No wind, no brass, no percussion. All the colour comes from how Elgar spreads the strings: high or low, divided or together, melody or accompaniment.

threads.title: Round in a circle
threads.body: The finale closes with the first movement’s tune, so the work ends where it started, a little brighter.
